maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I should like to make a few observations at this time. First of all, I should like to clear up one little point. When I was speaking in the house' on March 24, 1947 on emergency powers legislation I made certain statements. I do not intend to quote everything that I said at
Transitional Measures Act
that time, but I do want to clear up a point raised the other evening by the leader of the C.C.F., the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). The hon. member used only the last six lines of the statement I made at that time. I said, as reported on page 1697 of Hansard:
The greatest production of hogs for market in the history of Canada was in 1944, and that rather on a sound economic basis as compared with some of the controls we'have developed in the later years. Out of a total of 8,863,178 hogs, 5,768,046 were produced in the prairie provinces where the grain was also produced to feed the animals. Alberta led all provinces that year, producing 2,981,940 hogs. In 1946, Canada as a whole produced only 4.465,161 hogs. May I also add that during 1945 there were in Canada some 6,760,000 beef cattle, and of that total 3,596,000 were in the three prairie provinces.
Without reading the rest I might say I went on to point out that to produce a select hog required twenty bushels of barley. A subsidy of 25 cents a bushel on barley would amount to $5. The subsidy on freight rates from given points in the west to given points in the east amounted to another $4, which made a total of $9 per hog in favour of the eastern producer. I was making the point that it was rather unfair that the man who grew the grain and fed it to animals on his own farm could not collect those subsidies. If the hon. member, having stated only the last six lines of my remark, is ready to say that these should be reinstated under the same regulations as before, I will give him the opportunity to stand up and state that to the house right now.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: I was dealing with the hon. member's remarks with regard to subsidies generally as I understood them. I would agree with the statement he has just made, that there is a great deal of unfairness to the western producer. But I understood from his summary that he was opposed to subsidies generally as not being in conformity with the best interests of the economy.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
When the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) was speaking yesterday-I may say that I have the greatest respect for him because he is a most successful farmer-he said that the group to his right were opposed to freight subsidies. When speaking on another matter six days earlier, on March 20, I stated that I favoured freight assistance to feeders in other parts of Canada. I have never heard any member of this group oppose that legislation at any time, either in or out of the House of Commons. I have
Transitional Measures Act

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Believes very largely.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
Yes. very largely. I hope our Socialist friends will give credit where it is due and acknowledge that this is a very fine gesture on the part of free enterprise. Some may say that they are able to do it out of their profits, but I find from a more recent issue of the Free Press that the milk board demands a public inquiry and the chairman of the board points out that the companies cannot continue to do this for very long because they have been working on a smaller profit than in any other part of the dominion. So that should dispose of any argument that it is being done because the profits are large.
As has been stated in this debate, there are many _ angry and frustrated people in this dominion today, more especially among the farmers. Last evening I followed the discourse of the right hon. Minister of Agriculture with considerable interest but found great difficulty in following his line of reasoning. My difficulty was not lessened when I read his speech in Hansard today He stated

Transitional Measures Act
at one point in his discourse that when we reached August 1 of this year-hon, members know' that that is the first day of the grain marketing year in Canada-delegations of farmers and farm organizations came to Ottawa and said that the grain ceilings should not be lifted. Then he went on to say that no one, including the farmers, had a right to expect that this price would be taken off during that period of two months-August and September-and that if there wras any difficulty it would only be between October 1 and October 21, when the ceilings were lifted.
My contention and that of most of the farmers with whom I have discussed this matter, is that if the ceilings were to be lifted it was good business to lift them on August 1. That would have been a matter of good business. You did not have to advertise the matter in July, but on the evening of the last day of July or the first of August the announcement should have been made. I reject the argument made by the minister last night. I argue that the farmers who got into this jam had a right to expect that if the ceilings were to be lifted they would be lifted on August 1, and if not that they would be continued for another year. They had no way of knowing anything different. Why he went back to September 15 and said that it might have been expected, I cannot see at all. In my part of the west the farmers were marketing coarse grains the first week in August and from then on.
There has been some controversy over who is responsible for holding the grain and how much grain has been marketed. According to the research department of the Searle Grain Company, in their pamphlet dated October 22, 1947, the amount of oats delivered from August 1 to October 17, four days before the ceilings were lifted, was 25,922,835 bushels, and the amount of barley delivered for the same period 31,906,698. I have seen other figures given elsewhere but I think that the research officials of the Searle Company are accurate in their estimates. Then if you compare the deliveries further east you will find that they compare very favourably with those of the previous year. The minister went on to discuss this matter and told of the consideration that had been given by several grain companies and pools to having some form of adjustment. I happen to know something about the pools in the province from which I come. I will hazard a guess now that the people who delivered to that pool may be reimbursed for about one-third of the loss they took when they marketed their grain during that period. I have seen some of the correspondence to which the minister 5849-15
referred last night between certain line companies and other officials, some of them pretty close to the minister and to this government, and when he says that the government are not in a position to give a lead I wish to say that most of these companies expected some lead from this government in that respect. Without special legislation these people who delivered their grain during the period will not be fully reimbursed-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: They did not expect it yesterday.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
I say some of them
were expecting it a few days ago. I do not know what the developments are in the last few hours. I know they are looking forward to a statement from some responsible minister just as soon as possible on that and many other agricultural matters, because they want to develop their plans for the coming year. There is no argument about that at all. One of my colleagues just reminds me that the third day has arrived when the parliamentary assistant (Mr. McCubbin) to the Minister of Agriculture said that a full statement would be given and everything was going to be rosy for the farmers of Canada. However, we are still waiting and looking for the promised land in that respect.
Last evening the Minister of Agriculture developed his argument, and I must say it was a bit difficult to follow him, because he tried to tie the value of almost all agricultural products to the wheat contract with Britain or to the price of wheat. I read many articles which showed that our price ceilings on barley did not bear a fair relationship to the price of wheat in that contract. I am not sure how the minister arrived at the conclusion to base his argument on the value of wheat in the contract, because it is agreed that the price of wheat in the contract is SI.55, as he rightly said, basis Fort William, whereas the open world price of Canadian No. 2 wheat is S3..35 today. There is a big difference between $1.55 and $3.35. He stated that when the price of barley got beyond $1.25 the people would feed their wheat. I know a lot of farmers who will not feed anything under the fulfilling of this agreement over a long period, but they are still hopeful and they certainly think that they are entitled to the prevailing world values of their products. There is a hundred per cent difference, and more, in these two prices at the moment. I am not sure, but I believe the Minister of Agriculture is a member of the wheat committee of the cabinet. He has made statements out west, and has asked: who knows anything about the world

Transitional Measures Act
price of wheat? I wish to say that our Canadian wheat board know that the committee has set this price-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: That is not the world price. The price the hon. member quoted is not the world price.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: It is the price at which Canada is selling its wheat on the open market to countries other than Britain.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: It is about fifteen or sixteen cents above the United States price.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
Certainly it is, but that is the price at which we are selling No. 2 wheat to countries other than the United Kingdom under the agreement, and it will average over S3 a bushel to all these countries. In fact I could take the time to give a list of the prices. I have the statement here. Therefore I was not able to follow the argument as to why these values should all be tied to the price of wheat under the United Kingdom contract.
Somebody said, and I believe it myself, the fact that we had embargoes against oats and barley going out of this country-we are not allowed to ship to the United States-resulted in a ceiling on the price of these grains. My argument is that if that be true, and I think it is, we have practically the same system with respect to our beef and all other agricultural products, and we have the same system of ceilings with respect to all these products. Perhaps that is why the minister has attempted to tie these things all together in that way.
A word as to the price of barley. It is rather strange that in two points just across the border, United States barley sells for slightly over a dollar a bushel higher than it does in Canada. That is the existing United States market at the present time. There is a big difference in our oats, and so it runs all through these items. I say there is a tremendous amount of dissatisfaction throughout Canada today with regard to this feed policy. I repeat that the producers and the feeders, all agriculturists throughout this country, consider that action of the government most inefficient a.nd unbusinesslike, and they contend that if the subsidies were to come off they should have come off on the first day of August, because it was not feasible to do it after that. It should have been done at that time. Since it was not done at that time they are entitled to some consideraion in the matter of reimbursement. I refer particularly to those who disposed of their coarse grains during that period.
(Mr. Ross (Souris).]
There has been some argument in past years as to whether the United States wanted our beef. I received a letter last year from the United Stated Department of Agriculture stating that they were always ready and willing to accept our beef. I have an article which appeared in the Free Press Weekly Prairie Farmer on October 29, written by Mr. Morrissey, in which he states that he investigated the situation over there and that there is a great market always available for our beef, the most natural ready market that this country has ever had or is ever likely to have for our beef products.
In the same address last night the Minister of Agriculture spoke of the price of wheat and pointed out that it was $1.55 under this contract. He said1 that legislation had been passed under which the producers will be paid $1.35, basis Fort William, for their product. This will average something less than S1.20 at the elevators in the prairie provinces. They receive a participation certificate. He also mentioned that an amendment had been moved when we were considering amendments to the wheat board act last year, asking that the initial price be $1.55. He might also have mentioned that an amendment was moved by members of this group asking for disbursement of the surplus of the 1945 crop, none of which comes under the United Kingdom agreement. I forget the figures now, but there are many millions of dollars surplus of the 1945 crop which, at that time, it was argued was going into the pool to make a five-year pool under the four-year contract. I have always argued that it was not good business to put that money in the pool. When the farmers planted their crop and harvested it they expected that any proceeds over and above the initial payment. based on participation certificates, would have been disbursed. I understand, that some consideration is being given to>
advance payments and that legislation will be introduced this year to give another twenty cents a bushel. I w'as never able to understand why the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) said last year that this could not be done until parliament met. I am not able to understand it yet. I am not a lawyer, but I remember the discussion (hat took place on the amendments to the hill last year. Section 22, subsection 3 of bill 23. amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board' Act. 1925. which was passed during the last session of parliament, said:
The board shall, with the approval of the-governor in council, determine and fix the-amounts to which producers are entitled per bushel, according to grade and quality undercertificates issued.

Transitional Measures Act
I would think certainly the government had authority therefore to make these payments immediately, if they wished, and they should have done so, and they should not have taken advantage, as the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) said yesterday, of certain other emergency legislation to bring in taxation without consulting parliament anyway.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
If the hon. member
reads the act-it is not before me at the moment

I think he will find it definitely states that the advance payment which is to be made is $1.35 a bushel. The quotation he has read is one which provides for making the payments on the other grades to correspond with that $1.35 a bushel, but the basic price is $1.35.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
That is quite right,
but there is a proviso in there which refers to order in council. Apart from that, in the disbursement of these other payments on the completion of the crop year, I do not ever remember parliament being consulted before the disbursements took place. The board received authority from cabinet council. I am sure of that. My point is this:	the
argument was that this money was to be all pooled and left in the pool until 1950. I remember asking the Minister of Trade and Commerce a question in this regard, to which he replied that if someone died and it was necessary to clean up the estate it could not be done until 1950, for the reason that all these funds, from 1945 to 1950, would have to be pooled because the disbursements could not be made until then. That was the argument of the government at that time. These payments should be made, and I think they could have been made before now. The 1945 payments could have been made without having them tangled up with this contract.
The ministers make much of the fact that there are to be disbursements to the extent of $200 million this year, but these producers should have been receiving more than that amount and they will not get all their own money or all that they are entitled to. They have sustained a greater loss than that figure, and that loss in these days is much greater. The difference between $1.55 and $3.35 is SI.SO a bushel, an amount which they are losing and which they might have been receiving in the open world market.
The minister and others have argued that, with the other 160,000,000 bushels on the open market, no one knows what would happen. I would point out, however, that 5849-151
there is a greater shortage of cereals in the world today than ever before, and consequently a greater demand, and we can guess what the situation would be.
I am not able to follow all the-resolutions that are forwarded to members and to the government. As I said a year ago, about the time that deal was being negotiated with Britain, I was receiving resolutions from farm gatherings in my riding; the majority of the farmers attending those meetings were pool members, and they had been asking for an initial payment, from 1945 and on, of $1.80 a bushel. If these farmers were in support of these resolutions I do not understand how they could be satisfied with less. I repeat, the majority of the farmers attending those meetings were pool members. I received one resolution today from a large gathering in Manitoba, and after setting forth all the difficulties that had to be met, the resolution concluded:
Therefore be it resolved that the government of Canada should at once reimburse those farmers for the loss sustained on coarse grains by this government action, and that the government of Canada should increase at once the price of wheat and other agricultural products at present controlled by the government to levels in line with world markets.
Resolutions of this kind are being passed all the time. I might refer also to the Winnipeg Free Press of Wednesday, December 10, which contains an editorial that I should like to quote in part, I admit that that paper carries a great many articles on what the Minister of Agriculture and the government are doing. This is an enlightening editorial. It appears under the heading "Mr. Gardiner and Prices", and deals pretty much with the dominion-provincial conference held in Ottawa some days ago, which was called to plan agricultural production objectives for the coming year, and of which we have heard nothing since. The editorial is rather lengthy-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: They are all in the report.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
I have not time to read them all. However, I should like to quote from this editorial:
The passage in Mr. Gardiner's speech occurs in an answer given by him to Mr. H. H. Han-nam, the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. Mr. Hannam asked this question:
There are two things we would like to know. Is our agricultural policy to be based on needs of the peoples of Britain and Europe or on dollars? Is our agricultural ecouomy to be on the dollar or the sterling basis?
22S
Transitional Measures Act

Then it goes on to give the minister's answer, and continues:
Mr. Gardiner's meaning is clear. Prices of the various farm products are related to each other and must be kept in balance. Some of these products-cattle for example-cannot be allowed entry to the United States market because the U.S. prices are higher than the United Kingdom contract prices. Farmers who raise hogs would also demand entry to the U.S. market; so would dairy farmers and finally so would the grain growers.
Thus the wheat agreement emerges as a kind of a strait-jacket binding not only the wheat growers but the whole agricultural industry.
The editorial then concludes:
Is it possible that the whole farming community, without knowing it, has been compelled since August 1946 to accept low prices just because of this wheat agreement? Is it the fact that the hog industry, the cattle industry, the dairy and the poultry industries all have had to suffer because the government made a bad bargain in wheat?	[DOT]
Mr. Gardiner's reported statement would answer-"Yes" to these questions. And if, as he declares, the removal of the emargo on cattle and their sale in the United States puts the rest of these contracts including the wheat agreement in jeopardy-no other answer is possible.
Hitherto it has been generally believed that the only victim of the wheat agreement were the wheat farmers. Evidently this is not so. On the basis that all farm prices are related and must be kept in balance, the whole agricultural industry appears to have been sacrificed to maintain this wretched deal.
That is just the summing up of their findings in that respect. I do not care what province you go into, you will find there a state of confusion among agricultural producers. I regret to say that the farmers are disposing of their best breeding stock in great numbers, as well as of their poultry flocks, and a state of disorganization and confusion prevails, from which it will take the nation a considerable time to recover so that we may get back once more to a basis of production such as we should have.
I have myself been condemned in editorials for my stand on the question of controls. I have stated that many controls are hampering production, and I repeat that statement because I believe it is true in many respects.
My time is almost up, Mr. Speaker, but before I conclude I wish to appeal again to the government, as I have done in many sessions, for the removal of embargoes against our cattle entering the United States market. I have given many reasons why we should enjoy that natural market. I have also urged the removal of restrictions against the entry into the United States of our agricultural products of all types. Before I left home I did
fMr. Boss (Souris).]
some checking up on prices. I understand that the nearest thing we have to automobile manufacturing in Canada is the Ford, and I would point out that a Ford sedan in the town in which I live-Melita, Manitoba; that happens to be in Canada-has been selling since November 18 for 81,905.50. For that same type of car at West Hope, North Dakota, United States, over the border from my town, the price is $1,577. That is quite a contrast.
During the war, around 1942, I was greatly concerned about the prices of cars in Canada as compared with the United States. At that time in the United States it took ten finished 1,000-pound steers to purchase a car, whereas, just across the border in Canada, it required twenty such animals to purchase the same type of car.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: What month of the year did the hon. member refer to a moment ago?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Since November IS. It was around the first of December.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: He is arguing for free trade.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
Call it what you like. I am used to being called everything by some of your supporters. That comparison, Mr. Speaker, is enlightening-ten steers in the United States as against twenty in Canada to purchase the same type of car. What do you suppose the difference is today? To purchase the same type of car it takes five such steers in the United States and approximately fifteen in Canada. In other words the ratio has gone up from two to one to about three to one. More than that, an American citizen can today clothe his family for less money than it costs the Canadian citizen to clothe a family of like size in Canada, with similar clothing.
I have studied the clothing of children from head to foot, both in the United States and in this country, since November 18, and I can produce catalogues and bills to prove that the situation is as I have stated it. I believe that we in Canada, living alongside such a nation as we find to the south of us, cannot continue to exist with ever-increasing economic disparity operating against us. I am convinced that the general income of citizens in the United States, as well as their standard of living, will continue on a considerably higher scale than existed during pre-war years. Their own economists declare that their standard of living in the future will be considerably higher than it was prior to the war, and I submit that it should be our ambition and our sincere

Transitional Measures Act
endeavour to raise the general standard for all citizens of Canada, considering the opportunities that we have in this country.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
I consider the present debate, Mr. Speaker, to be perhaps the most important that has ever taken place in this house, and by far the most important that will take place at tihis session of parliament. Despite the fact that you have the Geneva agreement and the austerity program, I think the meat of the whole problem today is contained in the bill now before the house and in the discussion that logically should take place on this bill.
It amuses me and amazes me at times to hear our friends to the right complaining about controls. What I should like to find out from them some time during the course of the debate is, what, controls? The Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) is piloting this resolution through the house asking for continuation of controls. After checking the thing over as best I can, I do not think the Conservatives have much to complain of in the matter of controls and I do not think the government has much to ask for in the way of continuation of the controls they now exercise. Rents, fats and oils, and foreign exchange, in fact the whole economy of this country, as far as the average producer and consumer is concerned, is completely uncontrolled. What we are suffering from today, and the reason why we have an austerity program in Canada, is that the government of this country is throwing the machinery of production andi distribution too quickly back into the hands of irresponsible individuals who do not know what to do with it. That is the problem which confronts Canada and the United States today.
There is one thing I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members. In this discussion, and in the general discussion that will take place in this house, we must realize that the time has gone by for playing politics.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Oh, I do not expect anyone over there to my right to understand that, because that is all they know. That is why they are folding up throughout this country. They are rattling the bones of free enterprise in a vacuum from which that system dropped a long time ago, but they have not discovered it yet. Wha-t we must realize is that there is a show'down in this world today. There are two contending orders of society with two different sets of economics. There is the socialist movement, which dominates throughout the wmrld with the exception of this North American continent, and which is offering the peoples of the world something that is new.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: A lower standard of living.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
I do not care what the hon. member for Comox-Alberni may think. He is entitled to think what he likes. But he must admit that the system he defends and stands up for has had ample opportunity to prove itself during the lifetime of all of us here. It has given us two wars in one generation, has slaughtered people indiscriminately, has made the greatest development the world has ever seen in the methods of destruction but it has not yet learned how to distribute the needs of life, bread and butter, to the ordinary peoples of the world. After that trial three parts of the world today lie in ruins, with civilization practically blotted out because of stupidity and greed on the part of that very system. It cannot be defended. The evidence is plain all over the world in the ashes of destruction.
What I am trying to focus attention on is that members of this House of Commons will have to remember that the struggle today is not between Liberals, Tories and so forth as it was in the past. To yourself and to your people you are going to have to answer the question, where you stand in this showdown; because you are at a period in the world's history where changes are going to be made, whether you like them or not. The question is whether you are prepared to make those changes in the reasonable and sensible way that the rest of the British empire has made them, and they are still going forward, or whether you are going to bring about on this continent the destruction which took place In other parts of the world because they tri i*. to hang on to something which no longci served the needs of the people. There is a showdown, and there is no middle course. You stand either in one place or in the other.
The reason why the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) - was obliged to announce an austerity program in this country is, in my opinion, simply this, that the government acquiesced in the swan song of the Tory party on behalf of big business "back to free enterprise".

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: That is a great excuse.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: I thought the hon. member was not going to talk politics.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
During the war, what did we have here? Free enterprise did not fight wars. Meighen said in the Senate that if there were
Transitional Measures Act

not any profits in war, there was nothing to fight for. Free enterprise could not make profits out of war, so they said, "We will leave it to the government. There is no risk capital in this. We cannot make any money, so we will give it to the government. We are free to work for profits in this faulty economic system of ours, -but when it comes to throwing away money, we will let the government throw it away in buying materials for war".

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Did not the socialist government of Germany start the war?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: There was never a socialist government in Germany, and no one knows that better than the hon. member for Calgary West. He was legal adviser to the mine workers of America in district 18 for many years and he knows the labour movement, or should know it. What you had in Germany -my hon. friend knows, and I know he knows it as well as I do-was the last stand of the capitalist system; the boss with the gun at the head of 'his workers, still taking the profits.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: The boss was the government over there.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: That system was built up by the Tories of Britain, the Tories of France and the Tories of the world through Hitler to maintain their privileged position. The hon. member for Calgary West knows that as well as I do. He happens to be caught in the machine today. Why he is there, he can best explain. I have my own ideas.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: I had better tell the hon. member that I was fired the other day.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: What I was trying to tell the house was that hon. members, those who are capable of thinking would have to re-arrange their thinking; for anybody who thinks today-

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Do you allow that?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: I do not mean that as an insult, because my observation in the house is that most members are just rearranging their prejudices when they think they are thinking.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
During the war free enterprise sat back; no profits as Meighen said, and Meighen should know. The government of this country then undertook planning. They allocated materials. They arranged wages,

too low in many cases. Nevertheless they took control there; they allocated materials; they told you what you were going to produce. They did a good job, but it was a planned economy to a large extent; and they controlled prices, with a system of subsidies that worked well. But we did more than that during the war. In addition to planning our own economy, stepping up our national income and all the rest of it, we worked with our allies. There was worked out a system of co-operation with our allies. The world was one world so far as the fighting of the war was concerned. The common danger gave the people of this country a national objective in the winning of the war and the fighting of tyranny and oppression. The people responded to that. But as soon as the war was over we forgot its lessons and, instead of continuing co-operation, understanding and planning, the controls were thrown off; we have set up again in world affairs, competition with our allies, and that competition comes largely from this North American continent.
Had we continued in the post-war period with the controls we had during the war- and we need them far worse now than we did when we were fighting the war-we would be in a much better position. In my view the war is not over and will not be over until its destruction has been repaired. Had we continued with lend-lease and with the gifts, as we made them during the war; if we had continued with co-operation with our allies and kept these elements of competition out of the way, I believe the continent would be well on the road to recovery. All we would be contributing in the post-war would be materials to put our allies back on their feet, so as to show them that we are still allies and recognize their problems. Life would not have to be sacrificed. If we could do all these things during the war, why could we not have continued them into the post-war period? But we did not do that.
I believe this continent is in much more danger now than it was in 1939 or 1942. I think we are smack up against a decision which members of the House of Commons will have to make. I listened to the debate with respect to the Geneva trade agreements, and while. I do not consider I know all about it, in my view those trade agreements are a dream of the future. I do not see any international trade today, and I think there will not be any for a long time to come.
What is happening with respect to shipments of bacon to Great Britain? We do not know whether they will be able to accept our shipments next year. Why? Because the price

Transitional Measures Act
is too high. Then, they are getting wheat from Russia in a bilateral trade arrangement. Canada must trade in that way, too, unless we are going to hook ourselves to the United States and mortgage this country for all time to come. The condition is not realistic. We are alienating our allies from us, the ones who fought the war with us and who were our best friends and customers. And we are doing all this for the benefit of some of our friends who are still sticking to the theory of capitalism as it existed before the war in respect of world trade, and in our internal economy.
That is not going to work. We have to think about it. I will vote for this measure, certainly; but let me say to the government that I am not at all satisfied with the manner in which they used the emergency powers given to them. What did the government do? For a beginning they threw controls off as fast as they could, and brought about the domestic situation now confronting us. Not only did they throw those controls off, but they are now asking for the continuation of the few that are left. Then, while they have been taking off controls they have scrapped most of the administrative machinery. While at one time there were 120 wartime prices and trade board offices across the country, today there are only five. If the government intends only to continue with the measure of controls it now has I suggest we would be much better off without any, and that we should insist upon bringing before parliament bills which would be passed by parliament, and also insist upon holding ministers responsible for them.
I am not saying that I would ask that at the present time; but I would say that if the government is going to accept responsibility for regulating the economy of the country, it should begin doing it and not just talk about it. Controls should be re-established, and the necessary machinery should be set up -because I believe it will be permanent machinery in the future. I do not think we can get away from it, because we are going to have to live in a world operating on that basis. Governments will be expected to do business rather than play politics, as they were expected to do in the past. Men are going to have to come to the House of Commons and take responsibility for doing business with other countries which are starting out on a policy of conducting their business along the lines followed during the war-but, for another purpose, the purpose of construction.
I am somewhat critical of the complete disregard by some members of the functions of democracy. I think, for example, of the milk
subsidy, which was removed despite a vote of the House of Commons. I do not think any government, or any member of it, had authority to remove that subsidy when parliament was not sitting. The result was the price of milk has increased to the point where children cannot get it to drink. Farmers are not producing as much milk as they did before. They are confused.
If we are to expect the people of Canada to respect the institution and members of parliament, at least we must be consistent and show that parliament means something. Speaking to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) may I point out that under the Veterans Land Act the land requirement was placed at one-half an acre. That was the qualification placed upon a veteran who wished to build a house. The bill was passed in the House of Commons without a dissenting voice. After the house rose, someone in the government changed that provision and stepped up the requirement to three acres. That sort of thing does not create respect for the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: The statute gave that power by regulation.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
Yes, but it should not have been done. The bill should have stood as it was passed by the House of Commons and-should not have been changed until the members of the house came back and had an opportunity of obtaining an explanation as to why changes of that kind were necessary.
If we are to continue to keep the respect of the people we represent, then we must begin to show that the House of Commons is a responsible body, and that when it says something it means it. If controls are to mean the exercise of powers of that kind by the government, then so far as I am concerned I am not going to hand over the institution of parliament and its functions to any body behind the scenes.
A moment ago I referred to bacon deliveries to Great Britain. I have had meetings with farmers, of whom there are a considerable number in my part of the country; and I can tell the house that they are completely discouraged, even to the point of going out of hog production. This condition has arisen through the removal of the subsidy on feed grains. That applies not only to hog production, but also to the production of other livestock.
My understanding is that when the bonus on hog production was removed it was added to the selling price of the bacon we were shipping to the old country, thus stepping up the bacon price by one or two cents a pound. There is no doubt Great Britain is having great difficulties in the matter of obtaining her food
Transitional Measures Act

supplies; otherwise she would not be turning to other sources of supply. If we are going to think in terms of trading with other nations, then I do not think we can tie ourselves completely to any country because of the dollar sign. If we continue that road we will find ourselves isolated from the British empire, and I do not think that would be a good development.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: What bonus on hogs is the hon. member speaking about?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: All through the war the minister bonused hogs for the purpose of stimulating production.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: We have a premium on grade A hogs and also a premium on grade B, to improve the quality.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: That is a bonus, is it not?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: It is still on.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Does it apply to the whole country?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Just before coming to the chamber today I was informed by what I considered some well informed farmers that the bonus had been removed.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: It is still there, if you have the right class of hogs.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Take the question of fertilizers -and this all dovetails into the matter of controls.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
In order to make it
perfectly clear perhaps I should say that a premium was on by arrangement between packing companies and producers at the time the war started. During the war we put on a premium of S3 and $2, and this was changed some years ago to $2 and SI, which is still on.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
I thank the minister for
that explanation. During the war this country built up a considerable productive capacity. The members of this group have always contended that that productive capacity should have been reconverted and used for peacetime need. But that was not done. An outstanding example is the three fertilizer plants, one at Welland, one at Calgary and I believe the other at Trail, British Columbia. I understood from the announcement made in this house that the plant at Welland was going to be retained, but my information now is that these plants have all been sold for about half their value.
I am informed that fertilizer could have been produced in these plants for about $19

per ton on an average. Just before leaving Nova Scotia I met a number of very angry farmers who apparently were expected to pay $91 per ton for fertilizer, that is the ammonium nitrates. They simply cannot pay it and they are not going to farm. They told me that the people in Canada are going to be badly starved during the next year or two unless some drastic changes are made.
How can the Minister of Finance justify the mesa we are now in as far as our United States dollars are concerned when it is realized that seventy-five per cent of the productive capacity built up during the war has been sold to United States companies which are operating many of these plants today? We buy parts from the United States to assemble them in Canada, and those parts are paid for in United States dollars. Then the finished product is shipped to other markets and in many cases we are not paid for them. There is no reason why we should be in the present tangle as far as Canadian dollars are concerned. However, I am afraid we shall continue to be in that tangle until we realize that Canada is a nation, that we can stand on our own feet and compete with the United States if necessary.
I think the people of Canada would be willing to make some sacrifices if they had some incentive to build up this country for themselves. We should have a national objective such as we had during the war. Plant production should be developed for our own use. The man on the street is not as backward as he was in 1939. He realizes what this dollar crisis is and what brought it about. Then he sees that no changes are being made, that no leadership is being given or no objective is being set up whereby he can do something for himself. He is not ready just to tighten his belt and go through another austerity war in order that this country can be mortgaged to the United States. That is the sentiment that has been expressed to me right across this country.
There is no objective. That is why the farmers are confused. That is why the industrial workers are confused. That is why many people are confused. The world is completely changed; it is a new world. We must realize that and try to do something about it. I picked up a little news item a few days ago which I should like to read. It is as follows:
Cleveland, December 8 (AP)-Directors of Portsmouth Steel Corporation announced today the purchase of a non-eontinuous sheet mill with an annual capacity of 100.000 tons to bolster its critical supply of hot rolled sheets.
The plant is to be dismantled at Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, the directors said, for transfer

Transitional Measures Act
to Portsmouth, and was purchased from John P. Ludgate Associates of Pittsburgh for $275,000.
Scheduled to start production by the second quarter of 1948, the mill will produce carbon and alloy sheet specialties and will provide the foundation for a continuous strip mill, contemplated at a later date, an announcement read.
Why should a plant of that kind be dismantled in Canada and shipped to the United States? Why should a plate mill be standing idle-it is dismantled now because War Assets have sold it-in Sydney, Nova Scotia, when we are still importing plate from the United States? You are not fooling the people of the country one bit when they see that kind of thing going on. The steelworkers union is up in the air over the dismantling of this steel mill which is to be shipped to the United States in order to bolster steel production there, so that more parts can be sent to Canada to be assembled in Canadian plants owned and controlled by United States directors and financed by United States capital.
The answer is that there must be more government ownership of these plants. If risk capital cannot be found in Canada to develop our own resources, then I think the government will have to take the initiative and supply the necessary capital to build up our own economy and stand Canada on her own feet. I think we have one answer in the Polymer rubber plant at Sarnia. I believe this plant will go down in history as a monument to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) who followed it through and who I understand is still directing it. The plant certainly does not show any inefficiency as compared with any other rubber plant in Canada or the United States. It is a wonderful plant that is turning out a good product, and it is owned by the people of Canada. It must be remembered that we were pioneering in that field, but if it can be done with rubber, it can be done with other things. I do not believe we can solve our problems in any other way.
Then the question is asked, is there or is there not control? I want to tell my hon. friends over there that there certainly is irresponsible control in this country. My quarrel with the government is not over what they have done with their controls; I am critical of them for having given' up their controls. I think those controls will have to be re-established if we are to save ourselves from travelling a rocky road in the future.
What happened when the government threw off practically all the controls that had existed during the war? The result was that the control went from the hands of responsible people in this House of Commons to the hands of irresponsible people who acted behind 5849-16
the scenes, people who were not responsible to any one but their own boards of directors. I ask the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) whether or not there is price fixing in farm commodities? The price of everything that is produced today on a farm is fixed by Swift Canadian and Canada Packers. They dominate the picture very definitely, and the farmers know that. The farmers are told what they are going to get for what they produce. That is decided week by week in Montreal by the representatives of these two organizations. That is the kind of price fixing and monopoly control we do not want in this country. The whole of Canada depends on that industry, and if controls are necessary to protect the farmer and the consuming public, action should be taken through the board under the direction of the Minister of Agriculture, who in turn would report to this house.
Someone has said something about the control of wages, that we believe in the control of prices and that with it there should be control of wages as well. Are we not using the wrong terms in these things? Control striking people? My conception is that it is a matter of regulating your economy to get things in balance. It is not a matter of control. Control presumes something rigid, adamant, inflexible. My conception is that it should be a matter of regulation. I think the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made it very clear, as did the secretary treasurer of the Canadian Congress of Labour, that no one is silly enough to think that wages can skyrocket to any peak and not affect prices. Certainly we do not. It is one problem, as the secretary treasurer of the congress pointed out, and I have said in this house on many occasions that I want to see labour relations in this country established on a national basis under the federal Department of Labour so that we can get uniformity. Secondly, I want to see wages regulated through a national board composed of representatives of labour, industry and the government, who will sit down together and analyse their problems and come to an understanding with a view to getting uniformity right across Canada and getting away from this anarchy of strikes and nonsense where no one wins anything except misery. That is the way to offset it. That is the plan of this group and of labour right across this country. It is not a matter of controlling and regimenting the people at all. It is a matter of this house taking the responsibility for regulating the economy of this country in the interests of all concerned. You will not have a dictatorship as long as you have a free parliament and sensible members who will exercise their rights in this house. You may
Transitional Measures Act

make a mistake this time; you can change it next time. There is no suggestion of regimentation. All this nonsense you read about regimentation in the press is doing a disservice to this country and the United States in the troubled and mixed-up world in which we are living. It is making a lot more trouble quite unnecessarily.
There is another angle to price controls, and no one knows it better than the minister who is piloting this resolution through the house. I do not think it is possible to maintain price controls without a subsidy arrangement. The government, through the Minister of Finance, at the last session of parliament was adamant on that point. He said that they were continuing the subsidy policy no longer, they were finished with subsidies. I think it is nonsense for us to be talking about price controls now unless we can get a statement from the government as to their policy on subsidies. I think the time is ripe for that. The Minister of Justice made a statement on this question in the house last year when he said:
A subsidy policy at a time of grave danger of serious inflation is a valuable policy, in that it prevents the spiral of inflation from developing. If that spiral once gets under way it may carry prices to grave heights; and a judicious expenditure of government money by way of subsidy may result in a very much greater saving to the consumer in prices than the expenditure by way of subsidy.
I think the minister was absolutely correct in saying that, and as he is piloting this resolution, now, when there is an inflationary spiral in Canada, would be a very good time to test that theory, so that inflation may be checked and prices held or brought back to reasonable levels in relation to the earnings of industry and agriculture, through price control accompanied by a subsidy arrangement. That may be the fastest way out of our austerity program. I hope when the minister speaks he will say something on subsidies, because price control without subsidies is a vain hope. I do not think you can hold prices without subsidies.
I think every member of the house recognizes the grave position in which Canada finds herself at this time, and wants to do something to better conditions. But let us be realistic. Our talking here is not going to accomplish very much. You can say what you like, but after the house adjourns the cabinet has certain responsibilities and must run the country. We are living in a fluid world, with changes taking place day by day, and the cabinet must have authority to meet situations as they arise day by day when the house is not in session. If we recognize that

an austerity program is necessary in this country because of our foreign exchange position, and because of our whole internal economy being in a mixed-up state, I do not think there should be a dissenting voice in this house to granting the government power to maintain what controls they have until March 31 or whatever other period may be advisable. But let me say that I do not think the controls they now have are worth anything without subsidies. I believe they have to go back and do as they did during the war, everything with the exception of raising armed forces.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has placed on record six suggestions which I believe are all necessary. There are social difficulties; there are ups and downs, and it is a dangerous thing to take advantage of those circumstances to try to arouse the feelings of the people.

Mr. Speaker, the hon.

He would say that controls could not be constitutionally established because the British North America Act was illegally adopted and is of no effect. Therefore all the money that has been paid since confederation should be paid back. That was the most incredible performance and I can deal with it only in a jocular way in order to show its absurdity. When you demonstrate -that a proposition is absurd, everybody laughs. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Wylie) is sufficiently gifted to argue about the matter.
We have two systems or philosophies. We have the system of free enterprise which is also called capitalism and we have the system of socialism and communism. A short time ago the hon. member for Cape Breton South
(Mr. Gillis) made an eloquent speech, in which he said that socialism covers the world. That may not be -his exact expression but that is the meaning of what he said. Therefore, in his mind socialism must be about the same as communism because communism is the system that prevails in Russia and in the satellite countries of Russia.
Some of my hon. friends have tried to speak of private enterprise in a most contemptuous way. They have endeavoured to show that the man who is a capitalist must be dishonest. If the Social Credit party does not agree with the socialist party, in which I see so many old Liberals, it must be because their policy is capitalistic. Either the Social Credit party believes in private ownership, which is tied up with capitalism, or it does not. If the members of that party believe in the rights of private ownership, then they are in favour of free initiative and private capital. Otherwise, they are in favour of socialism. On the main issue there is no difference at all between the sound policy of the Social Credit party and that of the Liberal party.

speechtext: What is the difference between communism and socialism?

speechtext: I do not contend that I have much knowledge, and that is precisely one of the difficulties of the moment, that some people are a little bit too clever, and what is too clever is the part that is in excess of what they really are. speechtext: The communists.

No, not the communists. I see there men who have a Liberal background, men who were Liberals and whose families were Liberals for many years. Perhaps they found that everything was not going to their satisfaction in the prairie provinces and they thought they would try something else; they thought they would try the C.C.F. group.
I would remind them of what happened in England after Lloyd George and Lord Reading destroyed the Liberal party through their dealings in the Marconi affair and other matters and the efforts of Lloyd George to supplant Asquith and all that. What is needed in England today is not a socialist government; it is a good Liberal government which would carry on according to the Liberal traditions of England. There is a great gap between the Tories and the socialists in England, and there is no one to fill that gap because the actions of some Liberals in years past destroyed the party. But it should not be said that Liberalism cannot exist in England. If Liberalism existed in England today we would have free enterprise and England would not be at the mercy of other nations of the world; she would not be forced to ask for assistance like a poor woman. Letters that I have received show the results of the socialist policy in England.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: The Liberal policy.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
I am not speaking of the Liberal party; I am speaking of the socialist party that holds the reins of power in Great Britain at the present time. The condition of the people in Britain is pictured as rosy under a socialist regime, but actually it is very bad. 
I have received a letter which was mailed at Herne Bay, Kent, England, on September 22, 1947, in which the writer says:
Dear Sir:
Since receiving your very true letter in April I have written Mr. Strachey five times asking him to give us more of the food you so kindly send to this country, but all I get is excuses and no satisfaction. Well, my reason for writing to you this time is because I am asking you if it is possible for you and the Canadian government to put a ban on Strachey for letting our food go to thousands of foreign restaurants and cafes while we in our miserable homes see about one-quarter of what you send. Every foreigner in England is getting a better deal than any English person and I plead with you to demand that the food you send goes to the mothers and families of England. My daughter of seventeen is a lovely girl but she has lost a stone-
That is fourteen pounds.
-in weight. She gets up and goes to work hungry and comes home hungry. It is nothing but cuts and cuts in our food. I can tell you nine mothers out of ten are tired of trying to go on. Strachey is a dictator to this country-
A dictator, mark you, sir. I know he is.
-and the whole rotten government with him.
Rotten government. This is an Englishwoman calling Strachey's government a rotten government. She is a good Englishwoman and she is not afraid to tell the truth. Her letter continues:
We have one rasher of bacon a week each. For the rest we starve. The best fed people in this country are the government and the foreign twisters but the real English are downtrodden starved and-
Then a word is used to describe their condition which is awful.
I will now close, hoping so much that you and your gentlemen can make a law that the food goes on our tables instead of to the wrong people.
Thanking you,
Faithfully yours,
P.S. My daughter and husband have gone to work today on a slice of margarine each.
That is a letter I received from one lady.
I have another here which is just about the same. I have a number of letters like this.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: That is the result of the distribution of the food.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: That is the result of the government of England by socialists. We have that experience before us. The socialist party is like the Social Creddters.

speechtext: Heaven forbid!

They promise marvellous things. Now in Alberta-

speechtext: I do not want to be unpleasant to any member because the whole house is so kind to me. I appreciate that deeply and the house knows it. I am sincere in what I say and I thank my hon. friends for their words of encouragement.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member was sincere because if he was he would have to clean the communists out of his own government.

speechtext:
I have received many letters from Great Britain. I cannot read them all to the house; I cannot even carry them all in my pocket, but I have another one here which moves one's sympathy. It comes from a woman who is a councillor in her town. She has been a member of several delegations which have called on Mr. Strachey, and if the house is interested I shall read the letter. It comes from Essex and reads:
Sir,
I wrote to you some time ago and you so kindly answered, remarking of the sympathy you felt for us people having such a government with so many incompetent men.
Here I have enclosed a cutting in our today's Express.
The clipping is dated December 1, 1947.
I am shocked to think that people of your country receive such treatment. Heaven only knows what is going, to happen to this mother country of ours. People are starving. Everyone has a gloomy cast upon their faces. Day after day we feel hungry. Shortage of potatoes, petrol stopped for car owners, aged people getting less than anyone. God help our future generations if this sort of thing keeps on.
Christmas is approaching and we have nothing to look forward to
Strachey bought nuts and resold at 10 shillings per pound; tangerines, 5 shillings; apples, 2 shillings and sixpence. So what are the little children going to get? I look at my five children and wonder why should they suffer. A few years back we had plenty to eat, however poor one -was. Mr. Churchill never once got this country anywhere near the state it is in now, even when the enemy was on our back doorsteps.
I sincerely trust I am not boring you. You may be more conversant -with our state of affairs than ourselves.
With all best wishes,
Yours respectfully,
Mrs.

of men who are full of books, as my hon. friend said just a moment ago, men who are not practical but dangerous, men who may be geniuses. Plato was a communist. He was one of the greatest minds that ever lived on this earth. Others may be well gifted as my hon. friends are, but they are most dangerous because they are doctrinaires. A doctrinaire is a man who enjoys more the application of his theory, even if it is nefarious, than the welfare of his fellow citizens. That is why we find that these proud and conceited theorists are a danger to the world. They are a danger to the world because they want to apply their theories, not for the good of mankind, but for the personal satisfaction of their own ambition. I regret it. Some of them may be sincere. I appeal to those who have lived in the old country, those who have known Campbell-Bannerman, those who have known Asquith, those who have known Earl Grey of Falloden, those who have known the great Liberals who are now dead but will never be forgotten, those who have read the life of Gladstone, those who know about Morley, and other great men of England, those who have assured the supremacy of England. They must not be comfortable in the ranks of the socialist party, because the main role of the party is to deny, not only private initiative in terms of money, in terms of currency, but private initiative in terms of human freedom.

speechtext: No.
