speechtext:
I remember that one of my hon. friends disagreed with his leader. He was turned down. He was told something that was most unpleasant, something that I would not have suffered from any one of the cabinet ministers. But this is the policy of the party. It is, believe or die; believe anything that I tell you; it must be true. That is a very dangerous situation.
I remember that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) last summer spoke to the youth of this country. He made a wonderful speech. I entirely approved it. He said to these young boys who had been attending the lectures of professors who were trying to deform their minds, and unsuccessfully-and I say that is a tribute to these young men and girls who were there and who were bright enough to discern the truth in all the falsehoods that were told to them-"Let us be practical; let us look at the application of the theories that have been propounded by some people." Of course he did not mention the lecturers. He said, "Let us look at the socialist government that is now in power in the United Kingdom and see the result. The result is disastrous". My hon. friends are so

eager to forget liberty in their proposals that they would not admit that anything done by [DOT] Strachey is wrong, and that anything done by any of the ministers in the United Kingdom is wrong because the government is socialist.
I do not agree at all with Mr. Attlee, but I have a profound respect for him. I think he is a great man, but I could not say that of many of his colleagues. My hon. friends are ready to swallow them all, and they would protest vigorously if something was said about the incompetence of the government of the United Kingdom at the present time. But times have changed. Some years ago fanaticism was so thick and opaque that no member of parliament could have said that the government of England, even the present government was incompetent. If my hon. friends are scandalised by what I say I shall tell them only to remember what has been said by Mr. Churchill and not to forget the letters that I have just read to them which come from honourable, respectable and good women in the United Kingdom who suffer because of the despotism and stupidity of the socialist government over there.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
I am pleased to follow the hon. member who has just taken his seat and whose great grandfather, then member of parliament for Rimou-ski, gave up his seat in 1844 when the Hon. Robert Baldwin was beaten in York county, Ontario. The hon. member has a great deal of humour in his make-up, but there is also a whole lot of wisdom and common sense in what he says.
I am somewhat alarmed, Mr. Speaker, and also shocked when I look at this transitional bill. It is well named " transitional," as he will see. I wish to refer to three facts in connection with it. It has to do with chapter 16 of the revised statutes, bills of exchange and so forth. I will deal with the cause and effect of this resolution and the uses this transitional resolution is to be put to for the next six months.
I might say that this bill is well named. In 1896 Sir Wilfrid Laurier said that he was going to make Ottawa the Washington of the north. The government of the day has already made Ottawa the Washington of the north by the policies announced in this resolution and the Geneva charter. You cannot consider this one resolution by itself; they are all coupled together, this one, Geneva, the excise part, are all inter-related.
I should like to call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the effect of this resolution. The effect of it is simply this. Last Easter I said that our policy was one of " wait and see."

Transitional Measures Act
Our policy now is to wait and see what Washington is going to do. Before last February it was to wait six months to see what Geneva was going to do. I took my stand last spring when the Geneva meetings were held as I do now. The meetings opened in February and continued to the end of August. Had the dominions stood with the mother country they could have said to the United States government and to the others, preferential trade is a family matter of the British empire and admits of no controversy from without. Instead of that, what did we do? We surrendered all our political, financial, economic and military initiative to Washington, and now we are doing here the same thing, depending on and waiting to see what Washington does.
It will be nearly three years next Easter since the war ended, and all that this government has done has been to surrender in the Geneva pacts our power, military, financial and economic initiative to Washington. That has been the whole policy of the government; and its policy, in the measures we now have presented to us, is being laid down by Washington. Apparently the policy of the government is to wait and see what Washington will do, instead of waiting for six months or so to see what the outcome of the Geneva agreements will be. In the meantime, I should like to know how Britain is to be fed. She has only enough food for 27,000,000 of her population. Who will feed the other 20,000,000 when Britain cannot get the food she needs from Canada, her best customer, if contracts are ended?
Britain has been our best and, indeed, our only real customer. As I pointed out the other night, it was the opinion of the late Lord Bennett that Canada's welfare was wrapped up in the British preference and the British market, but now the government is evidently throwing the mother country overboard in favour of Washington. Our interests are now, it seems to me, identified with Washington, lock, stock and barrel. We are now committed to the United States economy entirely, and it is the greatest mistake in our history. The actions of the government have resulted in upsetting our entire economic policy as we have known it since confederation.
What use will be made of these Geneva agreements and foreign exchange acts? There will be another gamble in connection with our livestock, our bacon and eggs, our grain and our dairy produce. I am not criticizing the officials of the government. I am not one of those who criticize our officials, because I believe they are merely the victims of a
system. They have to carry out the orders they receive from the government. I suggest, however, that we should hold fast to the faith which is in us and which we profess and acquit ourselves like men. Let us stand by the British preference; let us hold on to the empire. The British empire with the dominions is richer in natural resources and in all kinds of raw materials than either Russia or the United States, and if we had elected to remain a part of the empire we shall do the only thing that can save Britain. But what are we doing? I contend, Mr. Speaker, that we are simply taking part at the present time in a gamble with Washington that will be fatal to the future prosperity of this country.
I fear that the effect of what the government is proposing to this parliament today will be to throw Britain overboard, and Canada, which was first in the diamond jubilee procession of 1897, will now be the last today.
Next to the united nations organization, these Geneva agreements are the most mis-, chievous proposals that have come before the people of the British empire or the world in history, and if they are followed to their logical conclusion, taken in conjunction with other agencies, Bretton Woods and the United States loan, it will mean the liquidation of the empire and the loss of our best customer. Britain will have to find other sources for her food supply than Canada when contracts are cancelled.
The loss of the British market is serious but the government apparently does not appreciate this fact. Britain is the only country that has afforded us a steady market for our meat, for our grain and food products, for our men, for our bacon and eggs in the past, and it is the only one that can save us now. What are we going to do when we lose the British market and find the United States raising embargoes against us? I predict that food costs will go up still higher in Canada. Canadian prices are going to reach an unprecedented high. It seems to me that we are showing very little faith in Britain after all that she has done for us, not only in the past, but during the last war, and I greatly regret the action that is being taken by the government. Apart from the position of the mother country, however, there remains the question as to where we shall find new outlets for our Canadian products, and in what countries other than Great Britain, certainly not in America.
The farmers of Ontario will suffer through the loss of the preferential trade which they have enjoyed. For seven years during the war Britain gave our farmers what amounted to their greatest prosperity, and if we remain
Transitional Measures Act

in the empire we can do a great deal to help Britain in her hour of need. The natural resources of Canada, New Zealand and Australia, together with the resources of the motherland, could provide the necessary supplies for the British people to enable them to get along until they can get on their feet again. That, however, does not seem to be the objective of the government.
I am absolutely opposed to the program submitted by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), because, as I say, in my opinion it represents nothing but a great gamble. Canada's policy is being laid down in the United States. The statements made by various ministers are certainly puzzling to me, as I believe they are others, and as I said the other day the action of the government will simply mean that Canada will become a Lazarus at the feet of Washington. But we do not know what will happen after the next ejection in the United States, though it is safe to predict that they will go in for high tariffs again. As a matter of fact, there will always be tariffs. By these Geneva and other agreements we have to all intents and purposes committed ourselves to Washington's economy, and that is not in the interests of the Canadian people. No government in Canada has ever had such powers as the present government has exercised in connection with these excise tax measures and all these other things, and it is my submission that the government should have obtained advice from some other source than the justice department. Before this session was called, there should have been a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada under the Supreme Court Act to see if it was legal. What the government did on November 17 in connection with foreign exchange is illegal. Such action to make it legal now will have to be passed by both houses of parliament; there is no doubt about that; and if a reference were made to the supreme court I have no doubt that the position I take now would prove to be the right one. But the government, by these orders in council on exchange, has gone over the heads of the law courts and of the House of Commons alike. We are simply wasting our time. These proposals of the government have been made retroactive to November 17 last, and all parliament does is to conduct a post mortem.
I suggest that we should change the name of this institution from the House of Commons to the house of coroners and undertakers, for that is all we are. All we have to do is to hold post mortems on these measures before us. We are just conducting proceedings as in a morgue. I can tell you this. That is one 
of the reasons why the popularity of the monarchy has increased so much as was evident in the recent empire marriage, with the corresponding decay of parliament, and the decline of the House of Commons and the present government by their measures are responsible for it. Talk about the family compact! The family compact, back in 1837, would never had dared to propose a measure like this which was brought into force on November 17, without the knowledge and over the head of the House of Commons, with regard ' to foreign exchange, as a result of which policemen have been stationed all along the border to see what you have in your pocket. That was done by the executive over the head of the House of Commons and parliament. The government is now proposing to make retroactive and legal what they did by order in council on November 17.
I believe that the Conservative party has been the pioneer party with respect to control. What do you call the national policy but control? What are controls but bonuses, subventions and subsidies, rvhich are the backbone of the national policy? My proposal for labour, industry and agriculture is to bring that national policy up to date and adopt the principles that I have suggested. My proposal is to bring in a national policy for grain that we are sending to the mother country and to our allies over there, and to bring in a national policy with respect to many other industries and callings up to date to meet after-the-war conditions. The whole Conservative policy that we have built up has that as its foundation. I propose that the national policy of the late Sir John Macdonald be brought up to date. I am for controls and subsidies for this winter on milk, bread and coal, but I should like to see the controls during the next three or four months adapted to our circumstances. I believe the day is not far distant when the people will wake up and the government will see that they have made a mistake. They have thrown away any hope of preferential trade. While I support the measure and extension to March 31 now before us in connection with the Transitional Measures Act, I should like to see this temporary control policy supplanted and instead adopted what one might call a long-term control policy for 1948, because the government seem to have had no vision having regard to what has been done in connection with these controls, such as is adapted to our circumstances. The government's policy is. "On again, off again, on again".	;

Transitional Measures Act
la the last six months everybody has been going to New York. What time have the ministers had to attend to their departments, when you have a whole carload of them going down to that farcical performance called the UNO which has just turned out to be a second Geneva? What time have they had to attend to these matters which are before the house at the present time? Why did they not do something long before this? Away back last spring they knew that we needed fuel and coal in September? They knew it in September and October. Fortunately we had a warm fall. Otherwise there would have been a great deal of suffering in the country. They knew that we needed controls with regard to food and milk; yet they threw them all away. I should like to see a long-term control policy adopted. There is by the United States in their loan policy coercion by Washington of countries that cannot pay such loans on any terms. I referred to this the other night. What I said will be found on pages 160 and 161 of Hansard, where I referred to the United States policy as shortsighted. None of the countries under lease-lend can pay them back. I said:
If successful, it can lead only to a repetition of the disaster of 1931, from which the United States suffered more than the rest of the world. Any loans which the United States grants to Europe on its terms cannot possibly be repaid, *while the loans will, sooner or later, be universally repudiated. Mr. Amery said that the fatal mistake made by Great Britain and, in large measure, by other countries had been its endeavour to conciliate the United States and facilitate the securing of its help by pretending to agree with the aims of the United States policy when we knew those aims to be out of date and impossible of fulfilment. The only way to avoid further misunderstanding and em-bitterment for all concerned, he said, was to speak frankly and to point out that, while grateful for such help as the United States may in her own interest care to give toward recovery, it must be free from all conditions which make that recovery impossible.
I regret deeply that the government have thrown over the preferential trade policy of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. Fielding and others, and have thrown away the principles of it. I believe that policy did more to save Canada during the depression in the thirties than any other. I believe that the people of Canada will some day wake up to find that out. As my former leader, Lord Bennett, said in his speech last June in the House of Lords when he saw the way Geneva was going with regard to trade pacts and the policy of the labour government over there, "The abandonment of preferential trade will mean the darkest hour in the history of the British empire, if not in the history of the world".
In conclusion, I wish to say that the present government's whole policy at Geneva is to be wrapped up in United States economy. It is part and parcel of it. Now we are tied up. We have not only financial but economic annexation to the United States. Let us look at what the government of hon. gentlemen opposite have brought before parliament. They are sending us all home now, after a post mortem on all these measures, and we might just as well be down in the morgue on Lombard street as here in parliament, discussing these pacts and Geneva agreements at a coroner's inquest. I think the people someday wall wake up. Nobody will wake them up now, bu-t they will have a re-awakening a little later on.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the people of Canada will be greatly disappointed in this December portion of the current session of parliament. The question has been asked a good many times; Why are we here? I begin to feel that we were called here in December, rather than six weeks later, simply to give the appearance of action-but it is only the appearance. So far as matters laid before us by the government are concerned, we are doing literally nothing in this period before Christmas.
To my mind it is even worse than that. Not only is parliament doing nothing with reference to the serious problems facing the Canadian people, but there does not even seem to be any recognition on the part of the government or on the part of the majority
Transitional Measures Act

of members in the house that there is, in the field of high prices, a serious problem facing the Canadian people.
The debate now before us, I submit, comes closer to that problem than, any other measure presented to us at this time. Even in this measure, which is only a resolution asking for the continuation of the Transitional Measures Act, there is little that we can do to bring home to the government the wishes of the Canadian people. Nevertheless this is the one debate in which it is in order to discuss the whole problem of price controls and subsidies, along with the other matters which are covered in the statute, the extension of which is being asked.
Despite the fact that there is that opportunity, there has been very little discussion in the debate on this important matter. I submit that it behooves parliament to keep pressing this matter upon the government until we get from the ministers something more satisfactory than the negative answers and excuses we 'have had thus far. I know the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is busy with other matters, but I do not think it is altogether fair that the minister, whose department should be dealing with this problem, should have been out of the house so much of the time when this resolution has been before us. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) is piloting t'he resolution through; but the matter contained in it which concerns us most is that which is uppermost in the minds of the Canadian people, namely, the high cost of living.
May I take just a moment to underline that which is well known, namely, why it is that the people back home are so concerned about rising prices? First of all, it has meant a lowering of the living standards of t'he Canadian people. In addition to the lowering of our living standards in a material way, it means a lowering of the health standards of our people. That is something the seriousness of which should demand our attention, until something is done about it.
Most of us in the House of Commons have homes and families; all of us know the problem it is, under current prices, to provide sufficient food to maintain proper health standards. Frankly I do not know how families with incomes of S30 or 835 a week-and there are some with less-manage to get along at all, to buy sufficient food so as to maintain their families in health and decency, to say nothing of the plight of pensioners and others on fixed low incomes. The fact of the matter is that, in years to come, Canada will pay for the lowering of our standards of health. Not only is there a lowering of health standards, but

there is being added to all the fears and insecurity people already have in today's world, the fear of economic chaos and the spiral of inflation in Canada.
I submit that it is not good enough for the government to keep on saying "no", as if there were any virtue in the consistency of that answer, and that it is not good enough to make excuses. Rather it is their responsibility to present to parliament plans for the economy of the country under which it can be regulated so as properly to distribute our goods and services with a view to proper living standards, adequate health standards, and some sense of security and stability in the minds of our people.
Although they do not seem to be revealing it,in the course of this debate, hon. members know that all kinds of organizations and people by the thousands back home are watching us with respeot to this one point. They think that is what this session was called for-to deal with the rising cost of living.
I am sure that every member has in his mail letters and resolutions calling for the re-imposition of price controls, calling for the re-institution of subsidies and other measures to bring down the cost of living. I shall not take time to read many of those I could bring before the house, but I do call attention to one received only today by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of this group. It would appear that similar letters were sent to the leaders of the other groups in the house, also to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) and to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). This letter comes, not from some ad hoc organization, not from any body whose political leanings might be suspect in the eyes of the government, but rather from the town council of the town of Port Colborne in the constituency represented by the Minister of Labour.
This resolution was passed unanimously at a meeting of the town council held on Monday, December 8. I shall not take time to read all the recitals which we find in the resolution, but the important part is in these words:
Therefore be it resolved that this council of the town of Port Colborne petition the federal government to re-iinpose controls and subsidies where necessary to roll back prices on basic consumers goods, of food, clothing and fuel.
There is the issue in a nutshell. There is the issue that the people of Canada expect this session of parliament to deal with. There is the issue placed squarely on the lap of the government. But instead the members of the government act like the French monarch who

Transitional Measures Act
said, "After me, the deluge." They act as though the whole thing has got out of their hand and there is nothing they can do. The Minister of Finance does say what the government will not do and gives his excuses, but he does not come forward with any plan for controlling or directing the economy of the country in the interests of the people as a whole. I suggest that it is high time the Minister of Finance had something more to say than simply to tell us that the party in power sits there with a mandate for decontrol. It is possible to interpret the platform of the Liberal party'at the last election in that light; but I point out that if the government is going to treat every item in its 1945 election platform as something for which it has been given a mandate, there are some other things for which it has also received a mandate from the people of Canada. It has a mandate to do something about housing, but it does not seem to be quite so concerned about that. It has a mandate for a national labour code, for which we are still waiting; it has a mandate for a national health policy; it has a mandate for decent old age pensions. We are still waiting for the government to fulfil these mandates as well as the mandate which ran through all its election literature of that year, the mandate for a new social order.
With regard to price control, I submit specifically that the government received a mandate in 1945 to continue price control as long as it was necessary. It is terribly obvious that it is necessary today, and if the Minister of Finance is going to talk about carrying out mandates, I submit that that is a mandate he should fulfil immediately.
Indeed there is one mandate which any democratic government always has, the mandate to pay some attention to the problems of its people, to pay some attention to the things that the people really want. I am sure hon. members generally realize how well this resolution of the town council of Port Col-borne, as well as similar resolutions which have been passed throughout the country, express the wishes of the Canadian people at this time.
We in this parliament also have a score to settle with the government in connection with this whole business of mandates. We have given the government wide powers with regard to price control and subsidies. The controls which were carried over from the war period have been continued from year to year. We did not give them those powers with the idea that they would be thrown away as soon as possible, but rather that they would be used, at least as long as they were necessary for
the well-being of the Canadian people. But we have received what amounts to an insult because the powers given to the government have not been used. I submit that that is not good enough.
It does seem a tragedy that there is no way in which parliament can obligate the government to do the things that parliament wants it to do. As far as the resolution now before us is concerned, we seem to have only two alternatives. We can vote against it, which would mean the end of all controls on December 31 and additional chaos on January 1. Therefore we will not adopt that alternative. The other alternative is to vote for it without any assurance that the government will make any more use of the powers that we are giving it than it has thus far. The only thing we can do is to avail ourselves of the opportunity to speak in this chamber in an effort to drive the matter home to the mind of the government.
There is only one thing we can do in the way of an amendment or vote. While it does not express all that some of us would like to say to the government, we of this group intend to take that action. Before I sit down I shall offer an amendment to the motion, the effect of which will be to extend the control measure, not just to March 31, but to December 31, 1948. I want to say immediately that when I offer that amendment on behalf of this group it is not to be interpreted as an expression of confidence in the way in which the government has handled price control since the end of the war. On the contrary, our saying that these controls should be continued in force, not just for three months, which amounts to nothing, but for a full year, is a way of telling the government that we believe that these controls should really be used.
In addition to that, we feel that extra time should now foe given so that some of the suggestions made this afternoon by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) might be carried out. The hon. member had something to say about the desirability of having permanent statutes passed by parliament which would look toward the planning of the economy of this country. If we extend the present bill for three months only and then come back and have another debate in February and March on the extension for another nine months, we believe that would be a case of getting nowhere fast. I submit that we should continue these controls for the full year which is possible under the provisions of the act. By doing
Transitional Measures Act

that, we would give the government time to bring before parliament statutes of a more permanent nature.
That is not the only reason for suggesting it. The immediate reason is that by the government's resolution the controls are to be kept in effect for only three months and the result will be that they are not likely to be administered very diligently. The tendency on the part of the wartime prices and trade board, who will feel they are going 3ompletely out of business in another three months, or at least that there is a chance of that, will be to wind up their affairs instead of implementing the principles of price control and subsidies as the people of Canada would like them to do.
I can imagine that the Minister of Justice who is piloting this measure might make certain objections to my proposal that the bill oe continued in force for the full twelve months of 1948. One of his comments might be that not all the orders in council under the control bill will be needed for the whole of 1948. The reply I would; make to that is that the government has the power under section 4 of the act to revoke any order in council which is no longer required, and in fact some orders have already been revoked. On the other hand, if the measure is allowed to lapse on March 31 the government would then not have the power to re-introduce any of the controls provided for in the act.
To say that we shall be able to see what is needed in February or March is, I submit, to suggest a further waste of time and another unnecessary debate in this house. There is no doubt about what the people of Canada want. They want the re-imposition of price controls and the re-institution of subsidies.
I submit that, in response to that demand, the government should accept our proposal that the act be continued in force for the full year and that during that period they change their policy of decontrol to one of re-control in order to try to meet the needs of the Canadian people. It is too serious a thing to allow our living standards to go down, to permit a threat to the health of the Canadian people and to create the danger of chaos and confusion in this country.
With the hope that the government will realize the urgency of this matter and in an effort to bring it- before the house as forcibly as possible, I wish to move, seconded by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson): That the word "March" in the seventeenth line and also in the next to the last line of the resolution be deleted and the word "December" be substituted therefor in each case.

The effect of that amendment would be to change the paragraph which reads:
And whereas it is considered desirable to continue the said act in force until the thirty-first day of March, one thousand nine hundred and forty-eight.
-to read:
And whereas it is considered desirable to continue the said act in force until the thirty-first day of December, one thousand nine hundred and forty-eight.
There would also be a change in the petition addressed to His Excellency the Governor General at the end of the resolution, so that it would call specifically for the extension to the control measure until December 31, 1948.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, much as I personally may be in sympathy with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I do suggest that any amendment which would impose a contingent additional impost upon the taxpayers is essentially out of order. It does not necessarily have to be declaratory of a direct impost or burden upon the people, but if it would have the possible effect of imposing an additional impost-I say with all respect that it is only possible; it may not be so-then such an amendment moved by a private member is, according to the rules of this house, out of order. The amendment declares in favour of a policy which might impose an additional impost upon the taxpayers of this country. Whether we agree with it or not, I am not arguing at all. But I do say this, that fundamentally, according to the rules of this house, the amendment is out of order because it does declare for the imposition of an additional impost upon the taxpayers of this country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I speak to the point of order raised by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie). He contends that my amendment might involve the expenditure of money and, therefore, would not be in order for a private member to move. I fully recognize the rule that prevents a private member from moving a money resolution. I contend, and I think I can prove to my right hon. friend's satisfaction that this is not a money resolution. The basis for my argument is standing order 60.
I will give my right hon. friend time to turn it up, although I am sure he knows it well. Standing order 60 reads:
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the house thinks fit to

Transitional Measures Act
appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
That is the standing order under which provision is made for the introduction of money resolutions. If one reads the citations that follow the standing order one finds reference to the phrase that ministers use when they introduce a money resolution to the effect that His Excellency has been made aware of the contents of the resolution and recommends it to the consideration of the house. I point out, Mr. Speaker, that any money resolution, according to standing order 60 and the citations that follow, can be introduced only by a minister, and three things must be done. First, the minister must announce His Excellency's recommendation; second, the resolution must be laid over for consideration at a future sitting of the house; and, third, it must be referred to the committee of the whole house.
If my amendment asking for a further nine months' extension of this resolution is described as a money resolution, then the resolution brought in by the Minister of Justice for a three months' extension is also a money resolution. But the Minister of Justice did not announce His Excellency's recommendation. He did not, when it was called under government notices of motion, move for its consideration at a future sitting of the house. He did not move for its reference to the committee of the whole house. I am not saying that he should have; I am glad that he did not. But the fact that he did not do these things means that, in his view, it was not a money resolution. It was something special. It was a simple direct petition to the crown. I submit, further, Your Honour, that the fact that you permitted the Minister of Justice to introduce this resolution without announcing His Excellency's recommendation, and the fact that you did not require it to be laid over for consideration at a future sitting and to be referred to a committee -of the whole house implies that, in Your Honour's view, it was not a money resolution, but rather something special, namely, a petition from parliament to the crown.
And so. Mr. Speaker, since it was not a money resolution in the first instance, extending it further cannot make it a money resolution, and I submit that it is within the power of the house as a whole to amend this resolution as it sees fit, provided that it comes within the terms laid down in the act itself, which of course it does as indicated in the preamble to the resolution now before the house.

Mr. Speaker, seeing that we are in technical difficulties, I wish to make one or two citations which I might have used to put some obnoxious legislation out of action. I want to quote Bourinot 23, Fraser Valley No. 1. If it would not have been abusing my prerogative I would have ruled oleomargarine out of order.
I came three thousand miles to Ottawa, to 40 degrees below zero and four inches of snow to put myself on record on two subjects. As I have sat and listened to the debates in this house. I realize more than- ever what it means to be a Canadian and to have the great freedoms we enjoy under democracy. We fight for freedom of speech; but, having listened to the official opposition, I think we are overpaying them at that.
I came here to endorse the attitude ol the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who unfortunately is not in his seat at the moment, but whom I am glad to see present in the house. I hope he will live up to what he implied he was going to do. I was interested in his explanation, yesterday of what has been done in the past, but I wish to assure him that my riding, a rural riding, is not particularly interested in vrhat has happened in the past. We are very much interested in what is going to happen in the future.
I shall be very brief, Mr. Speaker, because I realize that more entertaining speakers are to follow me. I should like to quote from an official government publiration entitled
Transitional Measures Act

Farm News. I presume the taxpayers of Can-are paying for'it because it is issued under the authority of the Right Hon. James G. Gardiner and Doctor G. S. H. Barton. The item I wish to quote is headed "Government to act on feed grain prices," and reads as follows:
At the second day's session of the dominion-provincial agricultural conference held in Ottawa, December 1 to 3, Right Hon. James G. Gardiner, Dominion Minister of Agriculture, said:
"I am authorized to state that some action will be taken which will result in prices rising on products fed from grain which will take care in future of the increase brought about in feed costs through the removal of ceilings and withdrawal of drawbacks or subsidies."
In that connection, all I wish to say is that the people in my riding naturally hope to have a favourable decision made. Above all, we are asking the minister to declare a policy, and to declare it now, even if it is an unfavourable one, and not two or three months from now. In saying this, I speak with full authority from my riding and, I believe, from rural British Columbia. I believe that the Ontario and Quebec members agree with me in that. What we are asking particularly is that the decision and the policy be announced. If it is not favourable let the farmers know. We hope it will be favourable.
I wish to assure you, Mr. Speaker, and, through you, the minister, that in my province the poultrymen are being forced out of business, not so much by the prices, but by the fact that they do not know what the future holds for them. You cannot contract to sell your eggs on the British market at a certain fixed price, with a certain fixed price for grain, and then have the grain price go up but your contract price remain the same. I want to know what the policy is before I go to my own riding, and I am going home next Friday whether the house adjourns or not, because I believe in spending Christmas where every man should spend it, in his own home, and particularly in British Columbia. Before I go home I want to know, on uehalf of the farmers of my riding, what the policy is to be.
I now turn to the man in this parliament in whom I have the most confidence, namely, the minister from my own province. I know he has a more considered approach to matters this session than he had in the last one, and there is a reason why he should. Like the member for Fraser Valley the minister now at least has hopes. While the veterans in British Columbia believe that all veterans and all members of the legion in Canada will get better results if all legion affairs are' left to the veterans affairs committee which will be set up in the new year, yet I wish to point out

to the minister from my province and, through him, to the government, that the matter is too serious to wait. The veterans cannot wait until the findings of the veterans affairs committee are made known.
So far as I know, the basic pension was set in 1919. Is it fair to expect veterans to wait for the results of the findings of the veterans affairs committee which may not be made known until June or July of next year? I believe it all goes back to the War Measures Act, and in case I shall be called to order with a little advice I wish to impress upon the minister the necessity of arriving at a decision. A decision should be arrived at before we leave next week as to what exactly is going to happen to the veterans, at least temporarily.
One thing more, Mr. Speaker, and this certainly is in order. The people of my riding quite firmly believe that price controls should be re-established at least on the basic commodities under the War Measures Act. I cannot understand my hon. friends across the way who one year ago-

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about the amendment that has been proposed by the hon. member for Winipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I am sorry that the amendment has been proposed because I am afraid it will precipitate, and I am inclined to think it should precipitate, a considerable debate in the house.
It was not the government's intention to debate this matter of controls in this part of the session that is being held before Christmas. It was our intention to formulate our policy as to the extension of controls and put that policy before the house in the part of the session that is held in the early part of the new 3-ear. We simply ask for the extension until March 31, not with a view necessarily to the abandonment of all these controls on March 31, but merely to maintain the position in statu quo for the time being. We shall be in a much better position to make recommendations to the house as to what controls should be abandoned and what controls should be continued in the month of February or in the month of March than we are at the present time. I think it is hardly fair to the house to ask it to take that responsibility now under the circumstances.
I cannot ask my hon. friend to withdraw his .amendment, but I am afraid that I shall have to oppose it. On the other hand, it will be pretty difficult for us to regard this striking tribute to the government as a vote of nonconfidence in the government. It is really saying to this parliament and to the country that we are quite content to leave it to the government of Canada as to what controls they shall continue and as to what controls they shall abandon; as to what orders they shall rescind and as to what orders they shall continue on through the year 1948. I find it somewhat difficult, if the house wants to force these powers on the government, to look upon such a vote as a vote of want of confidence in the government. The only point is this. There may be a serious objection to passing this amendment now because of some constitutional aspects of the case. I want to know if the extension of these powers would Impair or possibly impair the constitutional validity of this act, and I shall try to get the advice of my officers in the next hour or two or in the next half hour to see whether there is any such possibility and, if there is such a possibility, I shall have to take a firm position against this amendment.
I wish to make it very clear again, as I tried to make it before, that we are not, in voting against this amendment, saying that we are abandoning controls on March 31. The whole spirit of these resolutions is that they are stop-gap resolutions, interim resolutions. They maintain the position as it would be if we had not met in December. I shrink from the prospect of a debate, lasting perhaps all next week, on the merits of these particular orders in council relating to a wide variety of matters, as to which controls may be necessary during the year 1948, or may not. Some of them probably can be dropped; some have already been dropped. Do not let us get into that kind of debate today.
We are met here for a different purpose, for the purpose of considering the emergency legislation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and I should like to get to that. This debate has lasted much longer than I expected it would anyway. I certainly expect a very considerable debate when we bring in our measure dealing with controls, but I should not like the house to embark upon a protracted debate tonight and Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of next week.
I have not had an opportunity of consulting the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) or many of my colleagues; but my position, and probably it will be the position of the government, is this. I will vote against the amendment, but unless I am satisfied that there is some real constitutional danger to the act, that is, that the validity of the act is imperilled by extending it to the end of 1948, I would not regard the forcing of powers on the government as a vote of want of confidence in the government.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
I am sure we do not want to initiate a protracted debate upon the amendment, and I do not propose to speak at any length. What I rose to say was that the amendment has been introduced tonight because of the emphatic "no" which we understand the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) gave today to a representative delegation which met him on the restoration of price controls.
We know that the emergency legislation to which the minister referred is of great importance to the country, but we also know that the question of rising prices at the present time, and the difficulties that arise in the homes of the people across Canada, call for decision, and in that sense these matters are matters of emergency.
We believe that price controls are necessary as prices go up almost day by day, and it is more difficult for the people to get the things
Transitional Measures Act

they really need. We know also that, coupled with price controls, certain subsidies should be restored. The Minister of Finance is in his seat and he can say whether or not this report is as correct as I take it to be from the name of the journalist which appears at the masthead. Perhaps I might read a paragraph from it:
About seventy strong, the delegation met Mr. Abbott in his east block office to air grievances arising out of the continued rise in the cost of living. Mr. Abbott accepted the brief but indicated the government's answer to the whole contentious issue of restoration of price controls would continue to be "no."
It is because we feel that price controls will be necessary for some time at least that the amendment has been moved by my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
I might say a word in view of
the points raised by the hon. member for Ilosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I received this delegation from the consumers' league, or the roll-back-prices' group, this morning and I told them exactly what I told the house the other afternoon. I explained the reasons why I felt, and I thought the government felt that an over-all system of price controls was not practicable in Canada unless one were prepared to embark upon what I described as a completely controlled economy which would necessitate as well the imposition of wage and salary controls.

Mr. Speaker, the reason I rise in my place tonight to take part in this debate is that I have received a number of protest letters from my constituents and from different groups in my community.
The trouble in connection with controls has been that they were taken off at the wrong end. Controls on agricultural products should have been removed first, because they were put on first. Instead of that, however, they were the first to be imposed and the last to be removed. I am not complaining about the removal of controls, but I do complain that they were taken off at the wrong time; and I think even the government will agree to that now.
There has never been any group in our population which has gained more respect and admiration throughout the country than have the Canadian farmers. During the war, from one end of Canada to the other, they were congratulated upon the wonderful efforts they made in producing food. More than that, they accomplished that performance short-handed. Because of the high cost of labour, farmers were compelled to carry on as best they could without the aid of outside labour.
In many communities a census was taken and it disclosed that the average farmer engaged in agriculture was more than fifty years of age. That means only this, that many farmers operating farms were well over seventy years of age. Those men were not farming because they had to do it; they farmed because they felt they were doing a a job to help win the war, and that they should
continue until after the war was over. Today the war has been over for almost three years, and yet many of these men who have wanted to retire for some time find now that they cannot sell their farms at prices which would make it possible for them to buy houses fit to live in, in adjacent towns or cities. Prices of town properties are so high that they find it impossible to sell their good farms for sufficient to enable them to buy houses in the towns suitable to live in.
The result is that these men are compelled to remain on their farms. That is what I call an unbalanced economy. It just cannot work for any considerable length of time. The difficulty is that we have been taxed out of production. It is my belief that the producers of food should never have been charged income taxes, due to the fact that the}' have so many different problems to contend with.
For instance, crops are very uncertain. We have many good farmers everywhere doing a remarkable job. A good farmer will first prepare his seed bed as best he can to assure a crop and, if he is a good farmer he will pick the best seed he can buy. Again, he will sow his seed as early in the spring as possible and, by doing so, he feels he is reasonably sure of producing a crop. Then what happens? He may run into a dry year, or he may get a wet year as we had last year. Then he may have a good year with a heavy crop, but he is likely to wake up some morning and find that it has stormed through the night and his crop is pasted into the ground as though a steam roller had run over it. Very often he will lose half of such a crop when he tries to harvest it. The farmer never knows when he is going to be able to harvest a crop, and that is one reason w'hy.he should not be taxed on his income.
They have also been taxed out of production. This is true, not only in my section of the country, but in all sections. This applies also to other groups of the population. When labour was not receiving enough take-home pay last year its only redress was to go on strike. The result was that production fell at once. They were taxed out of production. After working four or five days, the working man refuses to go back to work because he knows he would be working for the government for the rest of the week.

That is the only thing that can and will pull us out of the mess in which we now find ourselves. Instead of Canada keeping up full production, we find ourselves resting on our oars waiting for the government to correct an error which they made a short time ago when they made it impossible for the farmers to make ends meet. The government has the choice of either raising the prices of hogs, cattle and eggs or supplying grain at a price where we can feed hogs, cattle and poultry at a profit. Farmers never got what they should have in my time. Prices were pegged during wartime and the farmers were not allowed to make much money. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on this resolution for the continuation of the Transitional Measures Act, 1947. I think it is generally understood now that, without the adopting of this measure, it would be quite impossible constitutionally for the federal government to control prices in this country. I for one feel that this power should be granted to the government for as long as they feel they need it, so that there would be no excuse then for not controlling prices. This measure will give the government power to defeat inflation, if they will, by the reimposition of controls which were so effectively exercised during the war.
I should like to commend now the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) who, during those war years, was the instrument through which those controls were effectively put to work. It is recognized that, should the federal government vacate this field of control now, the provinces, even though they may be willing, would be in no position to establish such a system, except perhaps in rental control. Interprovincial trade would militate against the success of controls of this kind, making them ineffective. The lack of trade barriers between the provinces would nullify the effect of any provincial legislation to control the 5848-17
high cost of living. Price control is definitely a federal responsibility and I think the people of Canada recognize it as such. Therefore, in the interests of all the Canadian people, power should be extended to the Canadian government to legislate in this field. The provinces may have the right in normal times to legislate on this matter, but even then the right would be useless without the existence of trade barriers between the provinces. Indeed it would appear that the Canadian constitution should be revised so that the federal government should have power at any time of emergency to control prices and apply subsidies where they are required.
May I express the hope at this time, despite all that has been said from the government benches, that the government will not neglect this opportunity which the adoption of this measure affords them to reimpose price controls and check the alarming increase in living costs.
The continued increase in the cost of living is, I believe, agitating the minds of more Canadians today than any other one thing. It is causing real distress in some quarters of this country, particularly to the disabled veteran who has had no increase in pension, to the old age pensioner and many others on low incomes. During the war, price controls proved effective, and rationing assured to almost everyone a reasonable supply of those essentials which are so necessary for a decent living. Those controls should have been maintained until production was adequate to supply consumer demands. Everyone ought to be aware of what happens when shortages prevail. Prices are certain to rise because people bid one against the other for the goods when they are offered for sale. The result is that prices jump and soon an inflationary condition develops. Only price control can handle such a situation. Advocates of decontrol have led the people to believe time and again that, freed from restrictions, business will serve the consumers just as well as, if not better than, under price control. They forget that it was under price control exercised by this government that Canada had the highest production in her history, and I am sure some of them today are painfully aware that, without controls, prices will reach fantastic levels as they have in the United States. You know, Mr. Speaker, United States business pledged that prices would be held once controls were lifted, but they did not hold prices. Prices rose alarmingly; profits in the United States today are
Transitional Measures Act

the highest they have ever been in the history of that country, and I am sure the story here is very little different.
The people most affected by the rise in prices are those on low incomes who are finding it increasingly difficult to make ends meet. Most of us can recall the distress and the suffering which constituted the unhappy lot of many people following the first world war. In western Canada sugar went as high as thirty-two cents a pound; flour was $6 a hundredweight; suits of clothes were $100 each, and shoes were $20 a pair. Most of us will also recall the aftermath of such inflation when in 1932, according to the Rowell report, the following prices were paid in Saskatchewan: oats thirteen cents a bushel; eggs, 8i cents a dozen, cattle $20 a head, and wheat, thirty-five cents a bushel. Surely Canadians do not want a repetition of that disastrous situation again. Only a reimposition of controls can prevent such a recurrence. In my belief, we are in a -fair way even now to realize the beginnings of such a situation. Prices in the United States are the highest in all time, and prices here are not very far behind. I sometimes wonder whether we are not too late even now to ask for the reimposition of controls to rectify the evil that inflation and too hasty decontrol have brought upon this country. As a matter of fact the great majority of the Canadian people have never asked for decontrol; therefore they cannot be blamed for the situation.
In January of this year sixty-six per cent of the people interviewed by the Canadian Institute of Public Opinion expressed disapproval of the federal government's decontrol measures. This represents a cross-section of the Canadian people and ought to be considered a fairly accurate index of public reaction. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there are many more Canadians today than that sixty-six per cent who realize that the price control line should have been held.
Everyone assumes that Canada has a democratic government which should reflect the point of view of the majority of the Canadian people. Someone has said:
In a democracy the people must be able to state in a definite manner the result they want in common; command obedience to their wishes from those who manage their affairs, their governments, and those who operate industry, trade and finance.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the people did state in no uncertain manner in that survey what they wanted in common. The survey has always been considered quite accurate. The government, therefore, has the support of the majority of the Canadian people, should it

restore price controls again. Indeed, if it does not, it seems to me that the government is not acting in accordance with the wishes of the vast majority of the Canadian public. One must assume that the government was stampeded into its present untenable position by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, which in January last called for the removal of price controls as soon as possible. No doubt they were also influenced by the social credit attitude as expressed by their leader on March 21 in this house when he said: "Social Crediters are implacably opposed to planned controls", and by the Progressive Conservatives who have repeatedly in this house called for the removal of all controls.
On the other hand, the C.C.F. requested the government on March 20 in this chamber to retain price controls to keep prices down, but were defeated by a combined vote of government, Social Credit and Progressive Conservatives.

That was the essence of the motion. I submit that this group was reflecting public opinion when that motion was presented to this house last March.
Recent events have proven without a shladow of a doubt that controls should not have been removed until a surplus of goods was available in this country. There is only one way by which the cost of living can be checked during the period the country is in short supply, and that is by the re-establishment of price controls and adherence to a scheme of subsidization. A serious situation has developed in this country-some people almost call it a national crisis-as a result of inflation. If we are to avoid a collapse of our economy such as that experienced in the thirties price control shoul 1 be reimposed immediately.

Transitional Measures Act
Certain interests in Canada argue that increased wages have forced decontrol of prices. But responsible people have known for a long time that prices advance first, forcing labour to demand higher wages. The increase in living costs is the most forceful argument used by workers and, Mr. Speaker, the only effective one, in their demands for increased wages. Higher wages are only a small part of the huge price increases which consumers are now forced to pay. Clothing prices in 1946, for instance, advanced twenty-two per cent, but wages in the textile industry increased only six per cent. Prices of consumer goods have always been out of line with wages.
In a bulletin released last year by the United States trade commission it was shown that for every increase in wages of one dollar in the United States, prices had advanced S6.50, or six and a half times as much. One might very well ask who obtained the difference of $5.50. Certainly not labour.
The situation in Canada is little different from that across the international border, except that labour here is not as well paid, which only aggravates the situation for them. The real reason why prices are high is revealed in the enormous profits enjoyed by big business as the result of decontrol of prices in this country. There seems no limit on the profit that they may make.
Corporation profits in 1947 in Canada are estimated at $347 million, an increase of 12^ per cent over those of 1946, according to a news dispatch appearing in the Winnipeg Tribane on December 3 of this year. Companies such as the Monarch Knitting made profits of 309 per cent in 1946 over those of 1945, according to the Ottawa Citizen of February 1. Building Products Limited, which deals in building material, showed an increase of 286 per cent in the same period of time, according to the Financial Post of March 1.
A host of other companies have made tremendous profits because of the decontrol measures of the government. In the face of such exorbitant profits, the government should reconsider its intention of abandoning the excess profits tax at the end of this year. Much the same interests blame the farmer unjustly for the high cost of living because of the seemingly high returns he receives for butter fat, eggs, milk, stock and grain. If this were a just charge, the answer to rising prices would be a reduction in prices paid for farm products. This would, however, be a most ridiculous proposal since many farmers can hardly make ends meet now because of the high production costs, and such a pro-
5849- 17*
cedure would only decrease production and! add to the difficulties of the present trying situation.
In many cases the farmer's margin of profit is less now than during the war years because' of the high prices he is required to pay for consumer goods. Scores of farmers are reducing herds, disposing of flocks of poultry, and even destroying young pigs because feed prices -are so high. There is no profit in these particular products. The lifting of the ceiling on coarse grains has made the situation even worse.
The government, in its haste to return to free enterprise, removed the ceiling control on coarse grains after most western farmers had disposed of their crops. About the only people-who have benefited from the action are the' speculators in grain and feed into whose hands a good deal of this grain had found its way. Speculation in this commodity promptly increased prices in these grains to almost prohibitive heights. Speculation of this kind is most unhealthy. If a large price is to be paid for coarse grains it seems to me that the producer who works and toils to produce the grain should have received the benefit and not a few speculators on the Winnipeg grain, exchange or anywhere else in the world.
President Truman, in a broadcast on October 5 last, stated:
The cost of living must not be a football to-be kicked around by gamblers in grain.
Most growers in the west desire the closing' of the Winnipeg grain exchange and insist that grains be marketed through the Canadian wheat board. I have received numerous resolutions and many other members of the House of Commons have received resolutions to this effect in the past few weeks. On the prairies, machinery, fuel, twine, trucks, gasoline and household necessities have advanced in price tremendously. The lifting of the ceiling on coarse grains has increased production costs to live stock producers and has benefited but few of the growers of these grains. The farmers' costs of production are rising because of the lack of price control on the goods they buy. Costs of production have in some instances almost doubled, but the ceiling still remains on the farmer's chief product, wheat.
I do not believe the farmer would complain if prices of consumer goods had been held down, but if everything he buys is allowed to advance because of decontrol, surely there is no justification for controlling the price of wheat. If the government is not prepared to re-establish price controls on consumer goods, then the farmer has a right to ask for a higher price for his chief product, wheat.

Transitional Measures Act

The farmer will not accept with good grace increased prices of the goods he needs if the present ceiling is retained on wheat. The farmer, and I believe that on the whole this is true, is not opposed to the British wheat agreement. On the contrary, he favours the stabilization of prices which such agreements permit. He is also anxious to retain the British market, so important to him in normal times, and the prices set for wheat were readily accepted when price control was in effect. But price control has now been abandoned and his cost of producing wheat is soaring.
There is a feeling on the part of many farmers that they have been double-crossed by the government by the decontrol of prices of consumer goods. I feel that controls should be reimposed or the ceiling on wheat removed, and I definitely prefer the former. This is the only fair thing to do. Canada must respect the wheat agreement, but the Canadian farmer must not be expected to carry more than his fair share of the load in rehabilitating Britain. The federal treasury should make up the difference between the price he now receives and the parity price which many farm organizations insist is substantially higher than the $1.55 f.o.b. Fort William that is paid. All Canadians should assist in the rehabilitation of Britain along with the farmers, and the federal treasury should come to the aid of the wheat producer in this matter. That is the only acceptable alternative to the reimposition of price control all along the line.
The C.C.F. supports the reimposition of price control because a large section of the Canadian people is on small incomes. A heavy burden is falling upon their shoulders by the high cost of living. In the United States, according to the federal reserve board, thirty-five per cent of those receiving incomes in 1946 either had gone into debt or had just broken even. There are no comparable figures in Canada, but conditions here are certainly no better and probably are worse.
Public opinion is demanding the return of price controls. The disabled veteran who fought for this democracy has a right to that protection. The old age pensioner struggles for existence without it, and the worker and the farmer are insisting upon it. On these grounds, the C.C.F. appeal to the government to take immediate steps to arrest the trend of prices by the re-establishment of price controls in order to curb excessive profits of corporations across this land and thus reduce the living costs for every Canadian. Only by developing a proper relationship between prices, wages and profits may this nation have economic as well as political democracy.
Mr. F. E. JAENICIvE (Kindersley): I have prepared some notes on the general topic of price control and on the disastrous results of the government's decontrol policy, but I have listened to all this debate and it seems to me that my colleagues in this group and the hon. member for Fraser Valley have fully covered the factual arguments in favour of control and the reimposition of controls. I desire to deal only with the legal and constitutional aspect of the matter.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) several weeks ago was reported in the press to have stated that it is impossible for this parliament to reimpose price control in peacetime, and he.said something to that effect in this house about an hour ago. With that statement I take issue.
I maintain, in the first place, that we have power to reimpose controls, as an emergency measure, war or no war. A few days ago we had a debate on the Geneva trade agreements, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and other speakers pointed out the importance of our foreign trade, the importance of exports. I agree generally with those arguments, and I do not think it is open to argument that the economy of Europe remains unstable at this time. As we are dependent to a great extent for our exports on the European markets, the Canadian economy must remain unstable as long as Europe remains so, and I think it will remain unstable at least until the end of 1948. I therefore suggest that there is an emergency, a grave emergency as far as our economy is concerned, because of the necessity of exports which now exists and which will exist for some time; and that, by reason of that, we have power to enact legislation to retain controls and to reimpose controls if this parliament so wishes. But I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that this parliament has jurisdiction over price control irrespective of emergency because I maintain that this question of price control is one that, by its inherent nature, is of national importance. I was sorry this afternoon to hear the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) have some doubts about the matter of the law in this particular case; because last March, in a speech which will be found in Hansard at page 1554, he gave to this house a fine exposition of the constitutional aspect of legislation in view of the decision of the privy council in the Canada Temperance Act case. It seems to me, however, that this important exposition of the law by the Minister of Justice, with which I fully agreed at the time, has not been fully appreciated by this house or by the country in general, because we still talk about an emer-

Transitional Measures Act
gency, andt say that there must be an emergency in order that this house may legislate upon such a matter.
The opinion of the Minister of Justice at that time was based principally upon the decision of the privy council in the Canada Temperance Act case. The important section of that decision was not quoted at the time, and I should like to place on Hansard a portion of it which I think will support the contention I am making, namely, that this parliament has power to legislate about anything that is of national importance, whether or not it encroaches upon the powers of the provinces. I quote from the Canada Temperance Act case as reported in (1946) 2 Dominion Law Reports, page 1; and I quote from the judgment of the Viscount Simon at page 5:
The first observation which their lordships would make on this explanation of Russell's case is that the B.N.A. Act nowhere gives power to the dominion parliament to legislate in matters which are properly to be regarded as exclusively within the competence of the provincial legislatures, merely because of the existence of an emergency. Secondly, they can find nothing in the judgment of the board in 1882 which suggests that it proceeded on the ground of emergency; there was certainly no evidence before that board that one existed. The act of 1878 was a permanent, not a temporary, act and no objection was raised to it on that account.
And here comes the important section of the judgment:
In their lordships' opinion, the true test must be found in the real subject-matter of the legislation: if it is such that it goes beyond local or provincial concern or interests ami must from its inherent nature be the concern of the dominion as a whole . . . then it will fall within the competence of the dominion parliament as a matter affecting the peace, order and good government of Canada, though it may in another aspect touch upon matters specially reserved to the provincial legislatures. I
I think this is the first time, Mr. Speaker, that the privy council has grasped the meaning of the words, "peace, order and good government" as they appear in the British North America Act. I believe the decision is a true interpretation of the attitude of mind of the fathers of confederation when they discussed the framing of our constitution. They were out to create unity. They were out to create a new nation. I do not think it is a question of centralization which is one that has always been raised in this house. I think it is a question of attaining the aims of the fathers of confederaton. What they had in mind was the unity of Canada, and this unity is very often confused with what some hon. members call centralization. I therefore maintain that, apart from the question of emergency, this
matter of price control goes beyond local and provincial concern because it is a matter which, by its inherent nature, must be the concern of the dominion as a whole. Therefore it falls within the competence of the dominion as affecting the peace, order and good government of Canada, though it may touch upon some matters reserved to the provinces under section 92 of the British North America Act. What proof is there that this question of price control is a national matter and not a provincial matter? I think the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) yesterday gave us proof of that when he referred to the Saskatchewan act passed by the provincial legislature last year, and in respect of which no action was taken; and he asked us why, although he supplied the answer. We are now beginning to know what it is like to live in Canada where the controls have been handed over to people whose only interest is profit. We have price control, but we have irresponsible price control, not in the interest of the Canadian family, but in the interests of the Canadian industrialist and the Canadian profit-taker.
I wish to point out to the government that when the people of this country, through their consumer associations, through their women's institutes, through their boards of trade, and through their wheat pool committees, plead with the government to reintroduce price control and subsidies, this is evidence of the fact that the Canadian people are beginning to recognize this as a method, not because they want a controlled economy, but because they realize that this is the only method which will give the results they need. So I would speak on behalf of the Canadian mother, the Canadian family and the Canadian consumer, although I have no belief that it will do any good. I believe that only elections convince the government of the need for action; and believe that these speeches are better made in the country where the people Still have the right to act. But I want to add my voice to that of the consumer associations on behalf of the Canadian family, in warning the government that this is a crisis. It is a crisis in every Canadian home. As the guardian of the safety of the Canadian people, the government dare not shirk their responsibility.
Right Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Veterans Affairs):	I wish to occupy
the time of the house for only one minute, Mr. Speaker. I must confess that I have been both bemused and bewildered by the last two speeches, the one delivered by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and the other by the talented lady member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum). May I say that this government has worked in anxiety and agony throughout the years of the war, 'by a carefully calculated policy of controls largely directed and inspired by the former Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) to keep the Canadian economy on a sound basis throughout the Dominion of Canada.

Why now throw it all
away?

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
Who interrupts? I
want no mumblings. If there are any interruptions I want them to be made so that they can be heard.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: The question I should like to ask is this. We all agree with what the minister says, but we want to know why the government is throwing away tlhat good work.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: I am indeed glad that my hon. friend agrees with that because it is incontrovertible. Just as that statement was incontrovertible, so is the policy that is now being pursued by my hon. and distinguished colleague, the Minister of Justice as he now is, in regard to price controls in Canada the safest and the sanest for the security, stability and solidarity of our Canadian nation.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext: Why drop it?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION IN FORCE UNTIL MARCH 31, 194S
speechtext:
My sentimental friend speaks about conditions in the home. Does she think for one second that each one of us has not equally at heart the welfare of the homes of our people? I have been in parliament for thirty years-and I say that not in a boastful way-and I know of no man who has a kinder heart or kinder feelings for the plain people of our country than has Jim Il'sley, the present Minister of Justice.
What are we arguing about, sir, may I ask? Why are we delaying this issue? We are all in agreement. We all agree that this resolution should go through. It is only a matter of whether we have it until March or until November or December or some such time as suggested by the agile and alert hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who always gets peculiar mathematical calculations introduced in peculiar amendments.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

The Minister of Justice liked it.

-and if we want it longer, I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will not be unvocal; I am sure the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum) will not be unsentimental; and I am sure the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) will not be uncynical. So let us pass this thing. Let us get on with the work. Let us pass this resolution right now and let us get on with the work of this session. Let us get on to the next business,* and let us get home next Friday night, so
that hon. members can join their beautiful families in their wonderful constituencies.
